titleEn: Happy is the one whose transgression is lifted away
progression: | C G | Am Em | F C | G C |
intro: Eleven verses on what silence costs and what saying it out loud is worth. The psalm names wrongdoing with three different nouns and uses all three twice, which makes it the cleanest place to learn the vocabulary of the confession: transgression as revolt, sin as missing the mark, iniquity as something bent. Watch the tenses turn at verse five, where the whole poem changes from past-tense illness to present-tense instruction, and watch who is speaking at verse eight, because it is not obvious.

stichs.en: Of David. A maskil.
Happy is the one whose transgression is lifted away,
whose sin is covered over.

verses.summary: The psalm opens on the far side of the story, with the verdict already given. Both descriptions are passive participles: nothing here is something the happy man did, only something done to what he carried.

stichs.en: Happy is the man to whom the LORD reckons no iniquity,
and in whose spirit there is no deceit.

verses.summary: The third term for wrongdoing arrives, and with it the one condition the psalm attaches to any of this: no deceit inside. The accounting verb is the ordinary one for keeping a tally.

stichs.en: When I kept silent, my bones wore away
through my roaring all day long.

verses.summary: The contradiction is deliberate: he was silent and he was roaring at the same time. The noise is the sound of a lion, and it is going on inside a man who is saying nothing.

stichs.en: For day and night Your hand was heavy on me;
my moisture was turned to the dryness of summer.
Selah.

verses.summary: The unconfessed sin is felt as weight and drought, not as guilt. A body drying out in the heat is the whole diagnosis, and the pause word closes the section before anything is said aloud.

stichs.en: I made my sin known to You, and my iniquity I did not cover;
I said: I will confess my transgressions to the LORD,
and You, You lifted away the iniquity of my sin.
Selah.

verses.summary: The hinge of the psalm, and the fastest reversal in it: the forgiveness arrives while the sentence about deciding to speak is still finishing. He stops covering, and the covering of verse one is what he gets.

stichs.en: For this let every faithful one pray to You at a time of finding;
surely when great waters overflow, they will not reach him.

verses.summary: The private case is turned into general advice, with a deadline attached: pray while there is still a time of finding. The drought of verse four is answered by a flood, and the flood is now the danger.

stichs.en: You are a hiding place for me,
You guard me from distress,
with shouts of deliverance You surround me.
Selah.

verses.summary: Address turns to God directly, in three short clauses that get longer as they go. The last one is strange and good: what encircles him is not a wall but a noise.

stichs.en: I will instruct you and teach you the way you should go;
I will counsel you, My eye upon you.

verses.summary: A new voice, and it is singular you, not the plural of the next verse. Whether God has begun speaking or the psalmist is now teaching from experience is the standing question of the psalm.

stichs.en: Do not be like a horse, like a mule, without understanding,
whose harness is bit and bridle, to curb it,
or it will not come near you.

verses.summary: The counsel arrives as an insult, and the point is control: an animal is steered by metal in the mouth, a person by understanding. The last clause is broken in Hebrew and every translation repairs it differently.

stichs.en: Many are the pains of the wicked,
but one who trusts in the LORD, kindness surrounds him.

verses.summary: The summary in proverb form. The many of the wicked answers the many waters of verse six, and the surrounding verb is the one already used of the shouts of deliverance.

stichs.en: Be glad in the LORD and rejoice, you righteous,
and shout for joy, all you upright of heart.

verses.summary: Four imperatives to a crowd, closing a psalm that began with one man unable to speak. The shouting here is from the same root as the shouts that surrounded him in verse seven.

pardes.body: Four movements. Verses 1 and 2 state the conclusion as a blessing on someone else; verses 3 to 5 are the case history, silence and drought broken by one sentence spoken out loud; verses 6 to 9 turn the case into instruction; verses 10 and 11 close with a proverb and a call to the community. The physical detail is the argument: nothing is said about guilt as a feeling, only about bones wearing out and sap drying up, so that speaking becomes a medical event as much as a moral one. Note that the covering he refuses in {{5.4}} is exactly what he is granted in {{1.5}}.

The three nouns of this psalm, transgression, sin and iniquity, are the same three that stand together in the thirteen attributes of Exodus 34, where God is described as lifting away iniquity, transgression and sin. The verb there is the verb here: {{1.3}} and {{5.11}} are both built on the root for carrying and lifting off. That is why the traditional English forgiven flattens something, since the Hebrew is about a load being taken off a back. Two other words are genuinely hard. {{4.7}}, rendered here as my moisture, occurs only a couple of times in the Bible and translations range from sap to vigour to the marrow. {{9.8}} is obscure enough that many versions do not translate it at all but rebuild the clause around it.

The unanswered question is who speaks in verse 8. If the voice is God's, the psalm is a dialogue and the instruction is the reward for confessing. If it is the psalmist's, then a man who has been forgiven immediately becomes a teacher, and the title {{1.1}} names what he is now qualified to produce. Both readings are old, and the Hebrew supports either, since nothing marks a change of speaker. The wordplay favours the second: {{8.0}}, I will instruct you, is built on the same root as the maskil of the heading. Read that way, the whole psalm is the lesson the heading promises, and the man himself is the syllabus.

The mystical reading works from the encircling. In {{7.7}} deliverance surrounds the speaker and in {{10.6}} kindness surrounds whoever trusts, both from the same root, so protection in this psalm is never a shield placed between two parties but an environment closed around one. Kabbalistic vocabulary later distinguished light that fills a vessel from light that surrounds one too large to enter, and this psalm is a natural home for that distinction: the man who could not speak was full of nothing but his own roaring, and what replaces it is not a filling but a circle. On this reading the deceit of verse 2 is the only real obstacle, because a spirit divided against itself has no outside for anything to encircle.
